$$
∀k\in (0,1),\,\overset{\text{scope of }∀k}{\overset{⏞}{n+{k}^{2}\ge {k}_{\begin{aligned} \\ ↑ \\ \text{b}\end{aligned}}}}

"question-0a806540-0634-5e11-9ba2-ff988650a653" :question/id #uuid "0a806540-0634-5e11-9ba2-ff988650a653" :question/math-academy-id "q-183877" :question/problem "Let $p\in Q$ and $q\in Q.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $∃\,p\in Q,\,2p=-1.$
- The truth set of the predicate $(\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1\,)$ is $Q.$
- $∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the statement 

$$
∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1
$$

from option III reads as follows:

$\,$ There exist rationals $q$ and $p,$ such that $p\cdot q=-1.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true, $2p=-1$ for some rational number $p$ (e.g., for $p=-\frac{1}{2}$).

- Statement II is false. For the predicate

$$
P(q):\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1
$$

we note that $P(q)$ is true for some $q\in Q$ and false for others. For example, 

$$
P(0):\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot 0=-1
$$

is false. However, 

$$
P(1):\,∃\,p\in Q,\,p\cdot 1=-1
$$

is true, since we can take $p=-1.$

- Statement III is true. The sentence 

$$
(\,∃\,q,p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1\,)
$$

 
can be written as

$$
∃q\in Q\,(\,{{∃p\in Q,\,p\cdot q=-1}_{⏟}}_{P(q)}\,)
$$

which is true whenever the inner predicate $P(q)$ has a nonempty truth set. And according to the discussion in statement II, this is the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d0f1732b-6bd9-5f1d-9035-c362872ddd7b"] :db/ensure 2792} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186152948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153431 :tutorial/content "We can apply quantifiers to predicates with more than one variable.

For example, the statement

$$\forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, n > m$$

reads as follows:

$\qquad$ *For all $m \in \mathbb{N},$ there exists $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $n > m.$*

This statement is true. Informally, it states that given *any* natural number ${\color{blue}{m}},$ there is an integer ${\color{red}{n}}$ that's larger than ${\color{blue}{m}}.$

- If ${\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{1}}\in \mathbb N$ and we select ${\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{2}}\in \mathbb Z,$ we have ${\color{red}{2}} > {\color{blue}{1}}$ which is true. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$
- If ${\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{2}}\in \mathbb N$ and we select ${\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{3}}\in \mathbb Z,$ we have ${\color{red}{3}} > {\color{blue}{2}}$ which is true. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$
- If ${\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{3}}\in \mathbb N$ and we select ${\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{4}}\in \mathbb Z,$ we have ${\color{red}{4}} > {\color{blue}{3}}$ which is true. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

And so on. It's easy to see that this statement is true since for any $m\in\mathbb N,$ we can simply select $n = m+1,$ and thus $n > m.$

**Watch out!** The order in which the quantifiers are stated is very important. If we swap the quantifiers in this example, we get $$\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m$$ which reads as follows:

$\qquad$ *There exists $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that for all $m \in \mathbb{N},$ $n > m.$*

This new statement has an entirely different meaning! Informally, it states that there is an integer $n$ that's larger than *every* natural number, which is false!

However, quantifiers *of the same type* can be swapped. For example,

$$\exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, n > m \: \equiv \: \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m.$$

Finally, if we have two or more quantifiers of the same type defined over the same domain, we can write only one quantifier followed by the corresponding variables.

For example, the (false) statement $$\forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \forall y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y$$ can be written more compactly as $$\forall \, x,y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y.$$

Similarly, the (true) statement $$\begin{aligned}∃x\in R,\,∃y\in R,\,x\le y\end{aligned}$$ can be written as $$\exists \, x,y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y.$$

We'll learn more about determining the truth value of a statement containing multiple quantifiers later in the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "992d8409-4fd0-588b-8307-afdd3dcaae09" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7942 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "df03f699-9bf6-5301-9f32-5a1b82728cef" :step/math-academy-id 145948 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152949}} {:db/id 17592186152949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152093 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151817 :question/id #uuid "aca83a15-ecdd-50ad-b384-b27d1f534497" :question/math-academy-id "e-12746"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d463a0dd-784d-55b6-a598-60819f5330d7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050884}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152453} {:db/id 17592186152454} {:db/id 17592186381467} {:db/id 17592186381804} {:db/id 17592186381845} {:db/id 17592186401790} {:db/id 17592186401797}] :knowledge-point/title "Translating Statements Involving Nested Quantifiers"} :step/id #uuid "7a975b0a-46f1-5b5b-b4d1-80613a1bc7ac" :step/math-academy-id 145949 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152950}} {:db/id 17592186152950 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153437 :tutorial/content "Consider the following quantified expression

$$\exists y \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, x > 0 \Rightarrow \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10 \, \big)$$

This expression has two quantifiers. The **scope** of each quantifier is the range in the expression where the quantifier is applied. We can use parentheses to avoid ambiguity in complex expressions.

In this example, the scope of the quantifier $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\exists y}$ is the following:

$$\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\exists y} \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, \overbrace{x > 0 \Rightarrow \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10}^{\textrm{scope of ∃y}} \, \big),$$

and the scope of $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\forall x}$ is the following:

$$\exists y \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, x > 0 \Rightarrow \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\forall x} \in \mathbb{R}, \overbrace{y < 10}^{\textrm{scope of ∀x}} \, \big).$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7034115f-f0c7-508f-8cdd-fd5c4a8380f7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7998 :tutorial/title "The Scope of a Quantifier"} :step/id #uuid "ac12610e-248a-5d1f-9e23-576263a1e1c9" :step/math-academy-id 145953 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152951}} {:db/id 17592186152951 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153449 :tutorial/content "The occurrence of a variable is called **bound** if it is placed right next to a quantifier or lies within the scope of a quantifier that uses the same variable. Otherwise, the occurrence is called **free**.

For example, let's examine the occurrences of variables in the following statement:

$$\forall\, m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N}, \, m > n$$

Is the statement true or false? To figure this out, we proceed as described below.

For example, the statement

$$\forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, n > m$$

reads as follows:

$\qquad$ *For all $m \in \mathbb{N},$ there exists $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $n > m.$*

This statement is true. Informally, it states that given *any* natural number ${\color{blue}{m}},$ there is an integer ${\color{red}{n}}$ that's larger than ${\color{blue}{m}}.$

- If ${\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{1}}\in \mathbb N$ and we select ${\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{2}}\in \mathbb Z,$ we have ${\color{red}{2}} > {\color{blue}{1}}$ which is true. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$
- If ${\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{2}}\in \mathbb N$ and we select ${\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{3}}\in \mathbb Z,$ we have ${\color{red}{3}} > {\color{blue}{2}}$ which is true. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$
- If ${\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{3}}\in \mathbb N$ and we select ${\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{4}}\in \mathbb Z,$ we have ${\color{red}{4}} > {\color{blue}{3}}$ which is true. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

And so on. It's easy to see that this statement is true since for any $m\in\mathbb N,$ we can simply select $n = m+1,$ and thus $n > m.$

**Watch out!** The order in which the quantifiers are stated is very important. If we swap the quantifiers in this example, we get $$\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m$$ which reads as follows:

$\qquad$ *There exists $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that for all $m \in \mathbb{N},$ $n > m.$*

This new statement has an entirely different meaning! Informally, it states that there is an integer $n$ that's larger than *every* natural number, which is false!

However, quantifiers *of the same type* can be swapped. For example,

$$\exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, n > m \: \equiv \: \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m.$$

Finally, if we have two or more quantifiers of the same type defined over the same domain, we can write only one quantifier followed by the corresponding variables.

For example, the (false) statement $$\forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \forall y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y$$ can be written more compactly as $$\forall \, x,y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y.$$

Similarly, the (true) statement $$\begin{aligned}∃x\in R,\,∃y\in R,\,x\le y\end{aligned}$$ can be written as $$\exists \, x,y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y.$$

[17592186152954 1063 17592186152095 17592186045585] [17592186153431 1064 "We can apply quantifiers to predicates with more than one variable.

For example, the statement

$$\forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, n > m$$

reads as follows:

$\qquad$ *For all $m \in \mathbb{N},$ there exists $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $n > m.$*

This statement is true. Informally, it states that given *any* natural number ${\color{blue}{m}},$ there is an integer ${\color{red}{n}}$ that's larger than ${\color{blue}{m}}.$

- If ${\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{1}}\in \mathbb N$ and we select ${\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{2}}\in \mathbb Z,$ we have ${\color{red}{2}} > {\color{blue}{1}}$ which is true. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$
- If ${\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{2}}\in \mathbb N$ and we select ${\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{3}}\in \mathbb Z,$ we have ${\color{red}{3}} > {\color{blue}{2}}$ which is true. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$
- If ${\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{3}}\in \mathbb N$ and we select ${\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{4}}\in \mathbb Z,$ we have ${\color{red}{4}} > {\color{blue}{3}}$ which is true. $\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

And so on. It's easy to see that this statement is true since for any $m\in\mathbb N,$ we can simply select $n = m+1,$ and thus $n > m.$

**Watch out!** The order in which the quantifiers are stated is very important. If we swap the quantifiers in this example, we get $$\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m$$ which reads as follows:

$\qquad$ *There exists $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that for all $m \in \mathbb{N},$ $n > m.$*

This new statement has an entirely different meaning! Informally, it states that there is an integer $n$ that's larger than *every* natural number, which is false!

However, quantifiers *of the same type* can be swapped. For example,

$$\exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, n > m \: \equiv \: \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m.$$

Finally, if we have two or more quantifiers of the same type defined over the same domain, we can write only one quantifier followed by the corresponding variables.

For example, the (false) statement $$\forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \forall y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y$$ can be written more compactly as $$\forall \, x,y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y.$$

Similarly, the (true) statement $$\begin{aligned}∃x\in R,\,∃y\in R,\,x\le y\end{aligned}$$ can be written as $$\exists \, x,y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y.$$

We'll learn more about determining the truth value of a statement containing multiple quantifiers later in the lesson." 17592186045585] [17592186153431 1065 7942 17592186045585] [17592186153431 1066 #uuid "992d8409-4fd0-588b-8307-afdd3dcaae09" 17592186045585] [17592186153431 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045585] [17592186153436 1064 "Consider the statement

$\qquad$ For all natural $m$ and $n,$ we have $m > n.$

Is the statement true or false? To figure this out, we proceed as described below.

The predicate $P(m)$ is false for all values $m \in \mathbb {N}.$ For example, $$P(1) : \quad \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N}, \, 1 > n$$ is false since we can take $n=1.$ Similarly, $$P(2): \quad \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N}, \, 2 > n$$ is false, since we can take $n=2.$ In general, it's sufficient to take $n=m$ for any value of $m.$ As a result, the truth set of $P(m)$ is $T_P=\emptyset.$

So, in our expression, we have:

- two occurrences of $y,$ both of which are bound, and
- two occurrences of $x,$ where one is free, and another is bound.

$$\exists \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{y} \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, \bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{x} > 0 \Rightarrow \big( \, \forall \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{x} \in \mathbb{R}, \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{y} < 10 \, \big) \, \big)$$

Distinguishing between free and bound occurrences is important since we are allowed to substitute values into free occurrences of variables.
